mcqs.question: A bundler removes an exported function from the final output because no importing file actually calls it. Which phase of the bundler's job does this describe?
options: Tree-shaking, part of the minify phase, which strips code no importer actually uses
Resolve, since it's about following import statements
Transform, since it involves changing the file's syntax
Split, since it changes which chunk the code ends up in
mcqs.explanation: Removing genuinely-unused exported code is tree-shaking, part of the minify phase that also strips whitespace and shortens names. Resolve is about locating files an import points to, transform is about compiling syntax (JSX/TS), and split is about grouping code into output chunks — none of those remove unused code.

mcqs.question: Why do bundlers typically separate a `vendor` chunk (React, other third-party libraries) from the app's own code, rather than bundling everything into one file?
options: Third-party code must legally be shipped as a separate file
Vendor code changes far less often than app code, so its content hash — and therefore its long-lived CDN cache — stays valid across many app deploys
Vendor chunks load faster than app chunks regardless of size
Bundlers cannot minify third-party code
mcqs.explanation: Separating vendor code means its content hash (and cache validity) only changes when a dependency actually updates, not on every app deploy — so users don't re-download React just because your app code changed. There's no legal requirement here, load speed depends on size not origin, and bundlers minify third-party code the same as app code.

mcqs.question: After a deploy, why does `main.a1b2c3.js` become `main.f7g8h9.js` rather than the same filename being overwritten in place?
options: The filename is randomly regenerated on every build regardless of content
The hash is derived from the file's actual contents, so any code change produces a new hash and a new filename the CDN/browser has never cached
It's a manual versioning convention developers type in by hand
The filename changes only when the file's size crosses a threshold
mcqs.explanation: The hash is a fingerprint of the file's contents, not a random or manual value — any code change produces a different hash, guaranteeing a fresh filename that bypasses stale caches automatically, with zero explicit invalidation logic needed. It isn't random, isn't hand-typed, and has nothing to do with file size.

mcqs.question: A team ships a new checkout flow's code to production behind a feature flag, disabled by default. What does this decouple, according to the feature-flag pattern?
options: It decouples deploying the code from releasing (enabling) it, so the deploy itself carries no user-facing risk and enabling it later is a config change, not a new deploy
It decouples the frontend build from the backend API version
It removes the need for code review on the new feature
It guarantees the new feature has zero bugs before release
mcqs.explanation: Feature flags separate the act of deploying code (which can happen safely with the flag off) from releasing it to users (flipping the flag), enabling instant, reversible rollout without a new deploy. It has no bearing on API versioning, doesn't skip code review, and doesn't guarantee bug-free code — it just contains the blast radius when bugs surface.

mcqs.question: Why does a server-side rendering (SSR) deploy typically need gradual rollout with health checks, while a client-side rendering (CSR) deploy usually doesn't?
options: CSR apps are always smaller in total size than SSR apps
SSR's deployed artifact is a running server process — it needs the same rollout/rollback discipline as any backend service, unlike CSR's swap of immutable static files
SSR cannot use a CDN under any circumstances
Health checks are only relevant to database deployments, not any frontend rendering strategy
mcqs.explanation: SSR deploys a live server process rendering per request, which needs the health-check and gradual-rollout discipline any backend service needs; CSR deploys immutable static files to a CDN, so a rollback is just pointing back at the previous build. Size isn't the deciding factor, SSR can still use a CDN for static assets, and health checks are broadly relevant to any running service, not only databases.

mcqs.question: A team applies the same `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000` header to `index.html` as to every hashed JS chunk. What breaks after the next deploy?
options: Nothing — index.html doesn't need to be re-fetched since its content rarely changes
The hashed JS files stop working because their hashes become invalid
The CDN will refuse to serve the new build entirely
Cached browsers keep serving the old index.html, which references the previous build's now-superseded (and possibly deleted) hashed filenames, serving a stale, potentially broken app
mcqs.explanation: index.html is the one file whose references change every deploy, so caching it long-term means users keep loading an old HTML file pointing at filenames from a previous build — the exact bug the asymmetric caching strategy (index.html: none/short, hashed assets: forever) exists to prevent. The hashed files themselves stay valid; the CDN doesn't refuse new builds; and index.html changing on every deploy is exactly why it shouldn't be cached long.
